name: Ellis Park Stadium
label: Ellis Park Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ellis Park Stadium' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/50638867: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Emirates Park' (296 m across).
notes: Rugby stadium, site of the 1995 Rugby World Cup final.

text.description:
Ellis Park Stadium is Johannesburg's great rugby and football ground, and the phone icon on the map puts you inside it, looking over the pitch from the stands. It is best known as the venue of the 1995 Rugby World Cup final, won by the Springboks. The ground was rebuilt in the early 1980s and holds almost 60,000 people. Its story goes back further: it was built in eight months on a former quarry and rubbish-dump site in Doornfontein, and the first test there was played in June 1928. It is named after J. D. Ellis, who helped make the land available.

From the seats, the stadium photographs well because of its scale. You can fit the pitch, the curve of the stands and the crowd into one frame, and on a match day the colour and noise of the supporters make the picture. Open-air concerts are also held here, which gives other chances for atmosphere shots.

The stands are not open to casual visitors. You need a match ticket or a stadium tour, and the rugby museum that comes with the tour is open on days without a match. If you only have access outside, the main stand facade framed by the surrounding Doornfontein streets is a worthwhile alternative. Rules on flash or larger equipment can apply during events, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Ellis Park Stadium is in Doornfontein, an inner-city district in the south-east of Johannesburg. It is the centrepiece of a sports area that includes Johannesburg Stadium, Standard Bank Arena and the Ellis Park Tennis Stadium.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so plan to arrive from Doornfontein or central Johannesburg by car or ride-hail. Ask to be dropped at the stadium entrance for your event or tour. Check current local security advice before you go, and avoid walking to the stadium on match days. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the pitch and the full sweep of the stands. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the crowd, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the players, banners or the far stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The best views come from the seats inside the bowl, which need a match ticket or a stadium tour. From the seats the photo shows the pitch, the full stands and the crowd. If you cannot get inside, the exterior view of the main stand facade, with the Doornfontein streets around it, is the second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the pitch markings up with them, so the horizon of the stands stays level. Keep some of the crowd in the foreground to show the scale. If you shoot the outside instead, step back far enough to fit the whole facade in and include a little of the street for context.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pitch to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or floodlights are washing out. Try a Live Photo on a match day to catch the crowd moving. Panorama can work for the whole bowl if you move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A match day gives the most atmosphere inside the stands. On a non-match day, the tour and museum give calmer conditions for photographing the empty seats and pitch.

text.access_note: Photos from the stands need a match ticket or a stadium tour, so check the official site before you go for access and any photography rules.

name: FNB Stadium
label: FNB Stadium
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/48848017: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'FNB Stadium' (425 m across).
notes: Calabash-shaped stadium that hosted the 2010 World Cup final.

text.description: FNB Stadium, also called Soccer City or the Calabash, is the big football and rugby stadium on the edge of Soweto, in the Nasrec area of Johannesburg. It was rebuilt for the 2010 FIFA World Cup, and the shape is meant to echo an African pot, which is where the nickname comes from. That is why it photographs so well. The outside is a mosaic of fire and earthen colours, with a ring of lights around the base that suggests a fire under the pot. Ten dark vertical lines also break up the stands. With a capacity of 94,736 it is the largest stadium in Africa, and it hosted the 2010 World Cup Final between the Netherlands and Spain. It also has a place in South Africa's political history. Nelson Mandela made his first Johannesburg speech here after his release in 1990, and a memorial service for him was held here on 10 December 2013. The stadium is so large that the main challenge is fitting it in. Stand back far enough to show the curve of the walls and the colours of the cladding, and keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines. Then move closer and fill the frame with the mosaic pattern for a second, more abstract shot. People walking past in the foreground help show how big the building is.
text.geographic_location: FNB Stadium is in Nasrec, bordering the Soweto area of Johannesburg. It stands next to SAFA House, the South African Football Association headquarters.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Nasrec, on the border of Soweto, and then for the stadium. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m north-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of the curved walls. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the mosaic cladding and the vertical lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The building is huge, so frame what is visible from there, moving only where access allows.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone level with the gridlines switched on so the walls do not lean. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full bowl and keep the lower edge of the frame just below the ring of lights. For a detail shot, zoom in on the mosaic colours and the dark vertical lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the cladding to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. If the lights around the base are on at dusk, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the cladding. Around dusk, the ring of lights around the base is easier to capture.

text.access_note: The area around the stadium may be open to walk around, but access may change on event days, so check the official site before you go.

name: Carlton Centre
label: Carlton Centre
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7098962123: the OpenStreetMap point 'Carlton Centre'.
notes: Skyscraper with the Top of Africa viewing deck.

text.description: The Carlton Centre is a 50-storey tower in the middle of central Johannesburg, and it is one of the easiest landmarks in the city to recognise. It stands 223 metres tall, and when it was finished in 1973 it was the tallest building in Africa. It held that title for 46 years. Today it is the fifth tallest on the continent, and The Leonardo, also in Johannesburg, now ranks above it. The tower is built of concrete with a grey granite finish, so it looks plain, solid and strongly vertical. That makes it a good subject for a phone, because the shape reads clearly even in a small picture. The complex also reaches a long way underground, with a shopping level below street level, so most of what you see from the pavement is the tower itself rising out of a city block. The tower is very tall, so the main challenge is fitting it in. Stand back as far as you comfortably can, switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and keep the phone as upright as possible. Switch on the gridlines and keep the tower's edges parallel to the vertical lines so it does not lean in the frame. Any people or vehicles at street level give a sense of scale. Keep your phone in a safe grip, as is sensible in any city centre.
text.geographic_location: The Carlton Centre is in the central business district of Johannesburg, on Commissioner Street. It is a large superblock of offices and shops that includes the tower.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Johannesburg, the central business district, and head for Commissioner Street, where the tower stands. Once you are on the street, the tower is easy to spot above the surrounding buildings. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the tower in from close range. Use the default lens (1x) from further back for less stretching at the edges. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the top floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, step back along the pavement as far as is comfortable, and use the ultra-wide lens until the full height of the building fits in your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn gridlines on and line up the tower's edges with the vertical lines. Hold the phone as upright as you can, because tilting it back makes the tower lean inwards. Include any people or vehicles at street level for scale. A 2x-5x shot of the top floors makes a good second picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky does not wash out and the concrete keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the whole tower is lit evenly. A clear morning or afternoon gives you a plain blue sky behind the tower.

text.access_note: The tower can be photographed from the surrounding public streets, but access to the building and any viewing areas may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Apartheid Museum
label: Apartheid Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/122486194: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Apartheid Museum' (285 m across).
notes: Leading museum on South Africa's apartheid history.

text.description:
The Apartheid Museum tells the story of apartheid and of South Africa in the 20th century. It opened in November 2001 and sits within the Gold Reef City complex in the south of Johannesburg. An independent non-profit organisation, Akani Egoli, set it up. The site is large, about 285 metres across, so there is plenty to photograph before you even go inside.

The outdoor parts are the easiest to shoot with a phone. The first exhibit is the Pillars of the Constitution in the courtyard, with one pillar for each of seven values: Democracy, Equality, Reconciliation, Diversity, Responsibility, Respect and Freedom. They make strong repeating lines, and their names are easy to read in a close-up. Further along, the Journeys exhibit uses large photographs of descendants of people who came to Johannesburg after gold was found in 1886. You first meet them from behind, as if walking the same way as you. Turn round after passing one to see the face. A photo taken from each direction makes a good pair.

Visitors are also given entrance tickets that send them through one of two separate entrances. This is part of the museum's design, and it makes a thoughtful frame for a picture of the entrance area. Take your time and keep your shots respectful, as this is a serious subject. Rules on photography inside may differ from outside, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the south of Johannesburg, within the Gold Reef City complex. It was built as an offshoot of the Gold Reef City Casino development.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. Head for the Gold Reef City complex in the south of Johannesburg. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the museum site, so once you are inside the grounds you are already there. Check the official site before you go for current access details. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the entrance area and the courtyard. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole width of the pillars. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the words on the pillars and for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Photograph outwards from there, then move to the courtyard to frame the pillars and walk the Journeys path to shoot the large portraits.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines. Line up the pillars so they repeat across the frame, with a person or two at the edge for scale. For the Journeys portraits, take one shot from behind and one from the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the nearest pillar or portrait, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the pillars keep their detail. Keep your phone steady and take a few frames in case of movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light, or an evenly cloudy day, usually gives a more even result than harsh midday sun. Weekday mornings are likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum, so check the official site before you go for opening arrangements, tickets and photography rules.

name: Gold Reef City
label: Gold Reef City
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Giant Wheel' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Giant Wheel' (pois).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Gold Reef City'.
notes: Theme park built around a historic gold mine.

text.description:
Gold Reef City is a theme park built on an old gold mine that closed in 1971. Its buildings are designed to look like the gold-rush town that grew up after gold was found on the Witwatersrand in 1886. That mix of replica streets, mine headgear and fairground rides gives you plenty of variety for phone photos. There is also a gold-mining museum in the grounds, and the Apartheid Museum stands on the same site.

The best view is from the top of the Giant Wheel, which guides name as the paid viewpoint option (check the wheel's location on the park map once you are in the park). From the top of the wheel you can see the mine headgear in the foreground with the park's rides around it. Behind them are the Johannesburg skyline and the old mine dumps. Guides call this the defining view of the park. They suggest late afternoon, and the wheel is a paid ride.

If you would rather stay on the ground, look for Shaft 14 (check the name on the park map). It is the headgear tower, and you can frame it against the sky with the rides around its base. Another option is the modern, minimalist entrance of the Apartheid Museum, which contrasts nicely with the replica gold-rush buildings. Some of these angles may need park or museum entry, so check the rules first. Photography on the rides themselves is generally not permitted, so check with the operators before shooting from the wheel. If you photograph people, ask first.
text.geographic_location: Gold Reef City is in the south of Johannesburg, south of the Central Business District and just off the M1. The Apartheid Museum is on the same site.
text.directions_text: Check the official site or a mapping app for how to get there, heading south of the Central Business District towards the M1. From there, the park is 222 m to the north-west. If you want the Giant Wheel view, check where the wheel is on the park map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the headgear, the rides and the skyline in one frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the skyline or a single piece of headgear. Use the default lens (1x) for everyday shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject. Mine headgear in the foreground with the park's rides around it, and the Johannesburg skyline and mine dumps behind, from the top of the wheel. Check with the operators before taking photos from the wheel.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the headgear in the lower third, so the skyline and sky fill the rest. Shoot a wide version and a zoomed version of the same view. For a ground-level alternative, try Shaft 14 (check the name on the park map) framed against the sky, with the rides around its base.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to set focus and lower the exposure slider a little if the sky looks washed out. Hold the phone with both hands and take several shots, because the wheel keeps moving. Only take photos from the wheel if the operators allow it, and keep a firm grip on the phone.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is the time guides recommend for the view from the wheel.

text.access_note: Gold Reef City is a ticketed theme park and the Giant Wheel is a paid ride, so check the official site before you go.

name: Market Theatre
label: Market Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lilian Ngoyi Street and Margaret Mcingana Street corner' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Lilian Ngoyi Street and Margaret Mcingana Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7138650728: the OpenStreetMap point 'The Market Square'.

text.description:
The Market Theatre fills a big Edwardian market hall in Newtown, a downtown suburb of Johannesburg. The steel frame was shipped from Britain and put up on site in 1913 to house the Indian Fruit Market, and its arches and dome were once ranked among the country's most important pieces of organic architecture. In the 1970s a group of theatre people raised money to restore the neglected building, with artists doing much of the work themselves. The theatre opened on 21 June 1976 and became known internationally as an independent, anti-apartheid stage. The Main Theatre was renamed the John Kani Theatre in 2014. Much of the original architecture and some of the old signs are still there, and Museum Africa shares the complex.

It photographs well because the old industrial hall is still easy to read. From the street corner you get the building's corner facade with the junction around it, which gives the picture depth and a sense of place. Stand back a little so the whole corner fits, then step in for details such as signs, brickwork and doorways. For a different picture, Mary Fitzgerald Square gives a view across open space with the theatre behind. Keep your phone straight and level so the vertical lines of the building don't lean. People walk past all day, so wait a moment for a clear frame.
text.geographic_location: In Newtown, a downtown suburb of Johannesburg, on the corner of Lilian Ngoyi Street and Margaret Mcingana Street. It sits in the same old market complex as Museum Africa.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is close by, so head for Newtown and come by taxi or hired scooter. From there the theatre frontage is about 1 minute on foot to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole corner facade and the junction into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view with less stretching at the edges. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for signs, arches and entrance details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Lilian Ngoyi Street and Margaret Mcingana Street (corner of the old market hall, facing the theatre's main frontage). The theatre's corner facade, the former produce-market hall, framed by the street junction.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them. Put the corner of the hall slightly off-centre and let the street lead the eye towards it. For an alternative, walk to Mary Fitzgerald Square and photograph the theatre across the open space, using the square as the foreground. Move in close to the eastern entrance for a detail shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Take a few frames, since people and vehicles pass through the junction.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the street is lively and the building is clearly visible.

text.access_note: The streets around the building are public, but performances, galleries and the interior may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Photography is typically not allowed during performances.
Street access in Newtown should be checked for safety, and daytime visits are the sensible choice.
Daytime is the best time for a visit and for photographs, because the street is busier and the facade is easier to see.
There is no Underground, train or tram stop close enough to give directions from, so a taxi or hired scooter is the practical way to arrive.

name: Johannesburg Zoo
label: Johannesburg Zoo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Zoo Lake' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Zoo Lake' (way/23370053): edge nearest the subject (1479 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23370079: large area 'Johannesburg Zoo' (1294 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large city zoo in Parkview's Zoo Lake area.

text.description:
Johannesburg Zoo covers 55 hectares and has been going since 1904. It sits in the same former park as Zoo Lake, which was given to the city for public recreation. Today it houses about 2,000 animals of some 320 species. It is also known for breeding white lions, a rare colour form of the African lion, and for its Siberian tigers.

For a phone photographer, the calmest picture of the area is from Zoo Lake, a short walk west of the zoo. From the lake shore you can frame water, grass and trees, with reflections that give a quiet, open view of the Parkview area. It makes a good change from shooting only enclosures. Inside the zoo, the pictures are close-ups of animals such as the white lions, so bring patience and use your zoom.

Start there for a wide scene, then walk east to the zoo if you want animal shots. Keep the phone steady against a railing or your own elbows, and wipe the lens first. Glass and mesh at enclosures can spoil focus, so get close to the barrier and tap on the animal, not the wire.
text.geographic_location: Johannesburg Zoo is in the Parkview area of Johannesburg, beside Jan Smuts Avenue. Zoo Lake lies just across the avenue, in the same former park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi or ride-hailing car, or drive, to Zoo Lake in Parkview, on the lake side of Jan Smuts Avenue. The zoo's main public entrance is on Upper Park Drive, at the corner of Jan Smuts Avenue. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the lake for water, trees and sky. Use the default lens (1x) for people and benches. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for animals inside the zoo.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Zoo Lake (Across Jan Smuts Avenue from the zoo; the lake shore side). The zoo's surroundings framed by the lake, with trees, grass and water reflections, giving a calmer landscape view of the Parkview area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on a lower line so the reflections fill the lower part of the frame. Put a tree or a person on one side as a foreground. For a second option, go into the zoo for close-ups of the white lions and other African wildlife. Keep your distance and zoom in rather than reaching through barriers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the far trees to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try portrait mode for friends with the lake behind them. At the zoo, use 2x-5x and tap on the animal's eye. Take a few shots, because animals move.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and calmer water for reflections. Check the zoo's current hours on its official site before you go.

text.access_note: Zoo Lake is a public park, but the zoo charges admission and may restrict photography in some areas, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hillbrow Tower
label: Hillbrow Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Constitution Hill' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Constitution Hill' (way/26352789): middle (478 m across); moved 25 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/764557028: the OpenStreetMap point 'Hillbrow tower'.
notes: Tallest structure in Africa's skyline of Johannesburg.

text.description: The Hillbrow Tower is one of two iconic towers often used to identify Johannesburg's skyline. At 269 m it was the tallest tower in Africa for 50 years, and it is still the continent's tallest telecommunications tower. Building began in June 1968 and finished in April 1971. It opened as the JG Strijdom Tower and was renamed the Telkom Joburg Tower in 2005. You can't go up it, as it has been closed to visitors since 1981, so the best you can do is photograph it from outside. That suits a phone well. The tower is a clean vertical line, and rising above Hillbrow's crowded high-rise blocks it gives a photo a clear sense of scale. The best-placed spot on this map is Constitution Hill, on the ramparts of the historic site, looking east toward the tower. From there the old walls frame the foreground, the tower stands up out of the apartment blocks, and the city skyline fills the background. The tower is some distance away, so it will look small at the default lens (1x). Zoom in to bring it closer, and keep part of the walls in the frame so the picture tells you where you are. Golden hour, early morning or late afternoon, gives the softest, warmest light. Yeoville Ridge, with Ponte City in the frame, and Melville Koppies, with green reserve vegetation behind the tower, are alternatives if you want a different view.
text.geographic_location: The tower stands in Hillbrow, a high-rise district of Johannesburg.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so check locally for the best way to reach Constitution Hill. Check locally before you go, and in the inner city consider a guided visit. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower itself. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a wider shot that includes the walls and skyline. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the tower very small, so use it only for a close foreground detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Constitution Hill (ramparts of the historic site, looking toward the tower). The tower rising over Hillbrow's high-rise blocks, framed by the historic walls and the city skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the tower on one third of the frame and let a section of the old wall fill a lower corner. Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it doesn't lean. For a second picture, try the default lens (1x) with more skyline on show. If you have time, Yeoville Ridge gives the tower with Ponte City beside it, and Melville Koppies puts it against green vegetation.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the tower doesn't turn into a washed-out silhouette. Hold the phone with both hands when zoomed in, as a small shake shows up more at 3x or 5x.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, early morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and warm.

text.access_note: Constitution Hill is a historic site, so check the official site before you go for current access and any ticket rules. The tower itself is closed to visitors.

name: Nelson Mandela Bridge
label: Mandela Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nelson Mandela Bridge' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/763928228: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nelson Mandela Bridge' (297 m across).
notes: Cable-stayed bridge linking Braamfontein and Newtown.

text.description: Nelson Mandela Bridge links Braamfontein and Newtown by carrying the M27 over a wide spread of railway lines just west of Park Station. It was completed in 2003 and is 284 metres long. It has two pylons, the taller of them 42 metres high, with cables fanning out to the deck. A distant view is the usual alternative, but the most interesting view for a phone is from underneath. Stand on the ground beside one of the pylon bases and look up. The cables and beams sweep across the frame in long, repeating diagonals, which looks striking even on a plain day. The bridge was built over 42 railway lines without stopping the trains, and from below you get a real sense of that scale. At night it is lit in rainbow colours, and the colours change for national commemorations. For a wider view, the Carlton Centre looks across the CBD skyline with the bridge in the frame. The bridge's own walkways also give views along the span. Traffic crosses the bridge all the time, so time your shots between vehicles. Visit with other people and in daylight if you can, as some visitors have reported feeling unsafe here, especially at night or when alone.
text.geographic_location: In central Johannesburg, spanning the railway lines west of Park Station and connecting Braamfontein and Newtown.
text.directions_text: Navigate to the bridge itself using the map. Once there, find the base of one of the two pylons and look for the spot on the ground beside it, using the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the cables and beams fill the frame from below. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tighter, less distorted shot of the pylon and cable details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the bridge's sweeping cable and beam lines, seen upward from below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Point the phone up and use the gridlines to line a pylon or the main cables up with the edge of the frame, so the diagonals lead the eye. Keep the phone level to avoid odd tilting lines. If you want the whole bridge and the skyline instead, the Carlton Centre is a recommended alternative, and so are the bridge's walkways.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then lower the exposure slider a little so the cables stay crisp against it. If you shoot after dark when the lights are on, use night mode and brace the phone against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is the best choice for both the view and your comfort. Go with other people, particularly if you want to see the coloured lights after dark.

name: Johannesburg Art Gallery
label: Johannesburg Art Gall.
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Klein Street and King George Street corner' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Klein Street and King George Street (our map tiles).

notes: Largest art gallery on the African continent, in Joubert Park.

text.description: The Johannesburg Art Gallery, often shortened to JAG, stands on the edge of Joubert Park in the city centre. The building was designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, with Robert Howden as supervising architect, and opened to the public in 1915. It has 15 exhibition halls and sculpture gardens. It was once the largest gallery on the continent, with more than 9000 artworks. Its collection includes pieces by Rodin, Picasso, Monet and Degas, alongside many South African artists. It photographs well because of its formal, classical front and the green park beside it. The original entrance faces south, and the 1940s east–west wings follow Lutyens' plans. The current north side is a later addition from 1986–87. From the corner of Klein Street and King George Street you can take in the street frontage in one go, with the edge of the park close by. Step back as far as the pavement allows so the whole width of the building fits in the frame. Then move in for a second shot of the columns and entrance steps. Look for people crossing the street or walking in the park to give a sense of scale. Joubert Park is in the inner city, so keep your phone in your hand only while shooting and put it away between shots.
text.geographic_location: The gallery is in Joubert Park, in the inner city of Johannesburg, on the corner of Klein Street and King George Street. The park edge is right beside it.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for Joubert Park in the city centre and make your way to the corner of Klein Street and King George Street on foot or by whatever local transport you use. Visit in daylight. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straightforward view of the front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or railings keep you too close to fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the columns and entrance steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Klein Street and King George Street (the corner where the gallery sits, on the Joubert Park side). The gallery's street frontage and facade from the intersection, with the park edge nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's top edge with a horizontal line so the front looks straight. Keep the building in the upper two-thirds and use the pavement or park edge in the lower third as foreground. For a different view, walk into Joubert Park and use the skeletal remains of the Conservatory as foreground, with the gallery behind. Look around on the ground to find them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone with both hands and keep a firm grip while shooting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daytime, when the street is busier and the light is even. Guides advise daytime visits to this area.

text.access_note: The street corner and park edge are public outdoor space, but the gallery's opening arrangements may have changed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Gandhi Square
label: Gandhi Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gandhi Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gandhi Square' (relation/21478985): middle (194 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26347068: 'Mahatma Gandhi', the best-known feature inside 'Gandhi Square' (192 m across).
notes: Central square with a statue of Gandhi as a young lawyer.

text.description:
Gandhi Square is a plaza in the middle of Johannesburg's Central Business District, and its main photo subject is the bronze statue of Mahatma Gandhi. The statue is about 2.5 m tall and stands on a plinth, with the restored Somerset House heritage building behind it. That gives you a statue with a historic backdrop in one frame. Benches around the plinth make it an easy place to stop and line up your shot.

The square has a story behind it. It was once called Government Square, then Van Der Bijl Square. In 1900 Field Marshal Roberts accepted the surrender of the city here. Gandhi had his legal offices at the corner of Rissik and Anderson streets nearby, and the statue was put up in October 2003. The square was renovated and finished in 2002, and the local bus terminal there has 24-hour security.

For photos, treat the statue as your subject and let the building sit quietly behind it. Take a few steps left or right until the statue's head is not cut by a window line or edge. For a second view, try Rissik Street, where you can show the open square in the foreground with the surrounding downtown buildings and the ramp to the underground parking behind. The statue is best seen from a little distance, so step back before you move in. Keep an eye on your belongings while you work.
text.geographic_location: Gandhi Square is in the Central Business District of Johannesburg, just off Rissik Street. Gandhi's old legal offices stood at the nearby corner of Rissik and Anderson streets.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so start from the central business district of Johannesburg and head to Gandhi Square, just off Rissik Street. The square has a local bus terminal, and guides say weekday parking can be tricky, so public transport is easier than driving. The statue is then about 1 minute on foot to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with Somerset House behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the surrounding buildings. If you prefer to keep your distance, use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the statue closer without walking up to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Gandhi Square (on the square, facing the bronze statue). The 2.5 m bronze Gandhi statue on its plinth, with the restored Somerset House heritage building behind it. For a different view, walk to Rissik Street and shoot back across the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the statue in the centre or on one third of the frame, with the heritage building filling the space behind it. Turn on gridlines to keep the plinth level and the vertical lines straight. Hold the phone upright (portrait) to include the full 2.5 m statue and the building above it. From Rissik Street, an alternative is to use a wide shot with the open square in the foreground and the downtown buildings and the parking ramp behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the bronze keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as people often walk through the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light is suggested for the statue.

text.access_note: Gandhi Square is an open public plaza in the city centre and no ticket is needed; stay aware of your surroundings and belongings while you take photos.

name: Johannesburg City Hall
label: City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rissik Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rissik Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/692307932: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Johannesburg City Hall' (146 m across).
notes: Edwardian civic building on Beyers Naudé Square.

text.description:
Johannesburg City Hall is a broad Edwardian building with a long colonnaded front and a domed tower rising above the middle. It was built between 1913 and 1914 and opened to the public in 1915. The style is described as Edwardian Baroque, with a portico of Ionic columns running the full width of the front and a half-domed entrance below the tower. It was made a National Monument in 1979, and today it houses the Gauteng Provincial Legislature. It photographs well because the columns give a strong repeating pattern and the dome gives a clear centre point. Rissik Street is also the building's main frontage, so you get the most direct view of it from here.

From here the whole facade fits in one frame, with the street and the granite steps leading the eye towards the dome. Check your phone's exposure if the sky is bright. If you have time, Market Street along the side gives a quieter view of the side and back of the building, with fewer people in the frame.

The building is a working government site and is usually closed and guarded, so plan on taking your photos from the street outside. Stay on the pavement and keep an eye on traffic while you line up the shot.
text.geographic_location: In central Johannesburg, on the eastern end of the old Market Square site, with its main front on Rissik Street. The Johannesburg City Library and Beyers Naude Square are on the far side of the building.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for central Johannesburg and walk to Rissik Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole colonnade and dome in one shot. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the dome and tower on their own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rissik Street (across the road from the main colonnaded frontage). The columned front of the City Hall with its domed front vestibule, framed by the street. Keep to the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on the centre line so the columns look even on both sides. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. Include a little of the street at the bottom to give a sense of scale. For a different angle, walk to Market Street for a quieter view of the side of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. If you take a panorama along the front, hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The front faces roughly east, so morning is likely to give the best light on the columns. Late in the day it may be in shade. Early on a weekend is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The building houses the Gauteng Provincial Legislature and is usually closed and guarded, so take photos from the street; check the official site before you go if you hope to go inside.

text.description:
The Absa Tower is an office skyscraper in the Central Business District of Johannesburg. Its full name is the Amalgamated Banks of South Africa Tower, and it is the headquarters of Absa Group Limited. It stands 31 storeys tall, which makes it a strong vertical subject among the city-centre buildings. It photographs well because it is a clean, tall shape that stands out against the sky, and it gives a clear sense of Johannesburg as a working business city rather than a postcard view.

The tower is best treated as a street-level subject. Start with the whole tower in the frame, then move in on the repeating lines of the upper floors for a more abstract shot. Look for a foreground such as a street, a sign or a passer-by, as it helps show how tall the tower is. Keep your phone upright and level so the sides of the building do not lean inward more than they must. This is a working office building, so photograph it from the outside and be considerate of people coming and going.
text.geographic_location: The tower is in the Central Business District of Johannesburg, the city's downtown business area, and is the headquarters building of Absa Group Limited.
text.directions_text: From there the tower is 130 m to the east, about 2 minutes on foot. Keep an eye on the map as you walk, as the tower should be in front of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the tower into the frame from close range. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the top floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject. The tower's modernist façade and its LED crown, photographed from the pedestrian walkways that link the building with Jewel City and Maboneng. The tower is about 2 minutes on foot from there, so you can also walk a little closer to change the angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the sides of the tower up with the vertical lines to keep it looking straight. Try one wide shot with some street in the foreground, then a tighter telephoto shot of the upper floors against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not turn white and the building keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, ideally in the afternoon, when the sun is behind you in the west and lights the side of the tower facing you.

text.access_note: The tower is a working office building and headquarters, so photograph it from the outside, and check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.

name: Constitution Hill
label: Constitution Hill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Great African Steps' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Great African Steps' (way/62129945): middle (78 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26352789: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Constitution Hill' (484 m across).
notes: Former prison complex that now houses the Constitutional Court.

text.description: Constitution Hill is a working court and a former prison on the same hill, which makes it one of the most thoughtful places to photograph in Johannesburg. The old fort was built by Paul Kruger between 1896 and 1899. It later became a prison, and Number Four, the section for black men, held Mahatma Gandhi, Robert Sobukwe and students from the 1976 Soweto uprising. Nelson Mandela was also held on the hill. The prison closed in 1983, and the Constitutional Court held its first session here in February 2004. The new court was built with bricks from the old awaiting-trial wing, and some of the old stairwells were kept as part of it. In 2024 the precinct became a World Heritage Site. For photographs, the best frame is the walkway called the Great African Steps. On one side are the rusting, weathered walls of Number Four, and on the other is the modern court building. Old and new sit in one picture, and that is the clearest way to show what the place is about. Also look for the Flame of Democracy, outside the court's wooden doors. It was lit on 10 December 2011. Take a few frames with people on the steps, as they give a sense of scale. For a different view, the exterior of the Constitutional Court is worth a photo on its own.
text.geographic_location: Constitution Hill is in Braamfontein, near the western end of Hillbrow, just north of Johannesburg's city centre. The hill looks south over downtown and north towards suburbs such as Parktown and Houghton Estate.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head to the Constitution Hill precinct in Braamfontein and check local options for getting there. The middle of the precinct lies to the south-west of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the prison walls, the walkway and the court in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the rusted metal and brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Great African Steps (walkway between Number Four and the Constitutional Court). The walkway framed between the rusting, historic Number Four prison walls on one side and the modern Constitutional Court on the other.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and use the walkway as a leading line, with the old wall on one side and the court on the other. Keep the horizon level so the walls do not lean. If you want a second view, the Old Fort ramparts look over the prison, Number Four and the city beyond, but they may be closed, so check with the precinct first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the weathered wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and pale concrete keep their detail. Avoid heavy filters, as the rust and brick already give strong colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the day is usually kinder, with softer light on the walls. Midday can leave harsh shade and bright patches on the walkway.

text.access_note: Entry to the precinct is ticketed and photography inside the Constitutional Court is restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mary Fitzgerald Square
label: Mary Fitzgerald Sq.
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mary Fitzgerald Square' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26346992: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mary Fitzgerald Square' (222 m across).
notes: Public square in Newtown, venue for events and concerts.

text.description:
Mary Fitzgerald Square is the open public space at the heart of Newtown, in Johannesburg. It was once a wagon site called Aaron's Ground. It was named in 1939 after Mary "Pickhandle" Fitzgerald, regarded as the country's first female trade unionist, because strikers often held meetings here in the early 1900s. Today it is the centrepiece of the Newtown renewal project, with the Market Theatre, MuseuMAfricA, the old Turbine Hall and the Workers' Library around it.

It photographs well for two reasons. The wide, open lawns give you room to step back and compose. From the lawns, facing west, you can frame the Johannesburg city skyline with the M1 bridge in view, with the green space in the foreground. Then turn your attention to the details: the installation of carved wooden heads and the lighting designed by Patrick Rimoux. Both make good close, street-level pictures, along with the murals and buildings nearby.

Plan on two or three different pictures from the same spot: one wide skyline shot, one closer shot of the carved heads and lit disks, and perhaps one of the surrounding architecture. The square hosts large events and markets, so it can be busy on some days. Check the event calendar before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Newtown, Johannesburg, close to the city centre. The square is surrounded by the Market Theatre, MuseuMAfricA, the old Turbine Hall and the Workers' Library.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Newtown, the area around the Market Theatre, and look for the large open square beside it. Once you are in the square, the phone icon on the map is on the open lawns. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the lawns, the skyline and the M1 bridge in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for the carved wooden heads and the surrounding buildings. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the skyline and the bridge, and for tighter detail on the heads and lit disks.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the skyline and the M1 bridge sit above the open green space of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the skyline on the upper line, so the lawn fills the lower part of the picture and leads the eye towards the city. Keep the horizon level. For a second picture, walk closer to the carved wooden heads and lit sky disks and shoot at street level, with the murals and buildings behind. They are also good for close-ups.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. For the carved heads, tap on a face to focus and check the shadows. Portrait mode can work for a close-up of one head, if your phone allows it on objects.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to be best for the skyline, because the sun is behind you as you face west. Choose a day without an event if you want the lawns clear.

text.access_note: Open public square, but it hosts large events and markets, so check the event calendar before you go.
